doc.title: Al Vollmer interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

title: Too shy to approach musicians: Omer Simeon, Charlie Gaines, Willie the Lion Smith
summary: He recalls the Eddie Wilcox band with Omer Simeon at winter carnival and Charlie Gaines in Philadelphia, regretting not speaking up, versus meeting Willie 'The Lion' Smith.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Do you recall any of the kinds of bands that might have played at social functions at Hamilton?

I remember one winter carnival. The pianist, whom I later met in Denmark, oh I can’t remember his name but he was the leader. Wilcox. Eddie Wilcox. And actually in high school I met Dot, who became my wife, and she came up for house parties. And I remember dancing with her because it wasn’t my class’s event. I think it might have been the senior ball or something, and it was winter carnival I think. And there was Omer Simeon in the band playing saxophone. And I knew it and didn’t dare — I was too shy, I didn’t go up. And oh the band got here two hours late. They got lost, there was snow, there was everything. If I had gone up to Omer Simeon, who I got to know later, in fact I have one of his clarinets. And if I had gone up to him he would have been flattered that someone knew him in the sticks of Hamilton College. And I didn’t do it. Same thing when I was at dental school in Philadelphia. On Walnut Street there was a club called the Cork Club, Charlie Gaines was playing there. And of course I knew Charlie Gaines’ name from those Fats Waller recordings, “Won’t You Get Off it Please” and “Harlem Fuss.” I didn’t go up and say hello to Charlie Gaines and I should have.
You know we — I know exactly what you’re saying because I had a similar instance —
Some of it comes from being European because I said who am I to go up and speak to these incredible people. That was one of the impediments.

And when you did, when you did, and you knew something about them, they were the most easy people to speak to. Yeah. I did that with one movie theater. Willie “The Lion” Smith was playing and I went up and spoke to him and he handed me his card and it had © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

Jewish writing on it. He was a cantor. So I mean, and then later on, because I had gotten to know him, he signed my book, the book that he wrote, yeah. So coming here, I mean it was kind of upside down you know. I had this hero image.
